idiom_name: if not ok: raise/return; walrus for check-and-bind
implementation_notes: Python's guard is an ordinary if plus raise or return, both documented in the language reference on simple statements; exceptions are the natural exit for caller errors (TypeError, ValueError, KeyError) and a bare return or a documented default for recoverable cases. What replaces the classic nested block is the assignment expression: if (match := pattern.search(s)) is None: return None checks and binds in one line, while EAFP style often replaces an explicit guard when the operation itself detects the failure more reliably than a pre-check. assert is compiled out under python -O, so it never validates input.
pitfalls: assert statements vanish under python -O; use explicit raises for anything that must always be checked.
Returning None as the failure shape is indistinguishable from a legitimate None; raise a specific exception type or return a documented sentinel object.
A try/except used as a guard can swallow unrelated exceptions; catch the narrowest type at the guard and let the rest propagate.
